equilibrium-intro-s1.title: Brown gas forming in a sealed flask
equilibrium-intro-s1.text: A student fills a sealed 1.00 L flask with colorless N2O4 gas at 0.0500 M and holds it at a constant temperature. The flask slowly turns brown as NO2 forms: N2O4(g) ⇌ 2 NO2(g). The graph shows the concentration of NO2, measured from the color, at several times.

equilibrium-intro-s2.title: One sealed container at four times
equilibrium-intro-s2.html:
Key: X2Y2XY

The reaction is X2(g) + Y2(g) ⇌ 2 XY(g). The temperature is constant and t1 < t2 < t3.

items.q: Which statement best describes the reactions in the flask at 20 s?
options: The forward rate is greater than the reverse rate.
The forward and reverse rates are equal, so [NO<sub>2</sub>] is constant.
The forward reaction runs by itself until the N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> is used up.
The reverse rate is greater than the forward rate, so N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> is being re-formed.

why.correct: A rising concentration of a product means the forward reaction is faster than the reverse reaction at that moment. The rates become equal only when the curve levels off.
options: Right: [NO₂] is still rising at 20 s, so NO₂ forms faster than it turns back into N₂O₄.
Equal rates would make the curve flat. At 20 s the curve is still climbing, so the rates are not yet equal.
This treats the reaction as one-way. As soon as some NO₂ exists, NO₂ molecules collide and re-form N₂O₄, so the reverse reaction runs from the start.
If the reverse rate were larger, [NO₂] would be falling. It is rising.

items.q: Use the graph to calculate [N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>] once the system has reached equilibrium.

mistakes.why: Value: you subtracted the NO₂ formed straight from the N₂O₄. Each N₂O₄ that reacts gives two NO₂, so N₂O₄ falls by half of 0.0400 M.
Value: 0.0200 M is how much N₂O₄ reacted, not how much is left. Subtract it from the starting 0.0500 M.

why.correct: At equilibrium [NO₂] = 0.0400 M. The 2 : 1 ratio means N₂O₄ fell by 0.0400 M ÷ 2 = 0.0200 M. So [N₂O₄] = 0.0500 M − 0.0200 M = 0.0300 M.

items.q: From 50 s on, [NO<sub>2</sub>] stays at 0.0400 M. Which statement explains why?
options: NO<sub>2</sub> forms and reacts away at equal rates.
The N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> has run out, so no more NO<sub>2</sub> can form.
The molecules have stopped colliding because the flask has cooled.
The concentrations of N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> and NO<sub>2</sub> have become equal.

why.correct: A flat concentration curve means the rate at which NO₂ forms equals the rate at which it is used up. Both reactions keep running.
options: Right: both reactions continue, and equal rates cancel in their effect on concentration. This is a dynamic equilibrium.
From the 2 : 1 ratio, 0.0300 M N₂O₄ is still present. It has not run out; it reacts as fast as it is re-formed.
The temperature is held constant and gas molecules keep colliding. Equilibrium is not a halt in motion.
At equilibrium [N₂O₄] = 0.0300 M and [NO₂] = 0.0400 M. Equilibrium means constant concentrations, not equal ones.

items.q: In a second trial at the same temperature, the student fills the same flask with 0.100 M NO<sub>2</sub> and no N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>. What is [NO<sub>2</sub>] once the system reaches equilibrium?

why.correct: Equilibrium can be reached from either direction. 0.100 M NO₂ contains exactly the atoms of 0.0500 M N₂O₄, so at the same temperature the system ends at the same mixture: 0.0400 M NO₂ and 0.0300 M N₂O₄.
options: Right: 0.100 M NO₂ holds the same atoms as 0.0500 M N₂O₄. Same atoms, same volume and same temperature give the same equilibrium mixture, whichever side you start from.
This assumes nothing happens when you start from the product side. NO₂ molecules combine to form N₂O₄ until the rates are equal.
This mirrors the first trial (0.100 − 0.0400) instead of reaching the same mixture. Starting from products, NO₂ falls to the same 0.0400 M.
This halves 0.0400 M as if the 2 : 1 ratio applied to the final concentration. The final mixture is the same as in the first trial.

items.q: Which feature of the graph shows that the system has reached equilibrium?
options: The curve becomes flat.
The curve passes through half of its final value.
The curve is at its steepest, at the very start of the experiment.
[NO<sub>2</sub>] reaches the starting value of [N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>].

why.correct: At equilibrium every concentration is constant, so a concentration-time graph becomes a horizontal line.
options: Right: a slope of zero means the concentration is constant, which happens when the forward and reverse rates are equal.
Halfway is just a point on the way up; the concentration is still changing there.
The steepest part is where the forward reaction most outpaces the reverse reaction, the opposite of equilibrium.
No such rule exists. [NO₂] levels off at 0.0400 M, below the starting 0.0500 M of N₂O₄.

items.q: Based on the diagrams, which is the earliest time shown at which the system is known to be at equilibrium?
options: t<sub>2</sub>
t<sub>1</sub>
t<sub>3</sub>

why.correct: Equilibrium shows up as a composition that no longer changes with time. The first two snapshots with the same counts are t₂ and t₃.
options: Right: the counts at t₂ and t₃ are the same (3, 3, 6), so the composition has stopped changing by t₂.
The counts change between t₁ and t₂ (XY goes from 4 to 6), so the system was still reacting overall at t₁.
The system is at equilibrium at t₃, but its composition was already the same at t₂.
At t = 0 there is no XY at all, so the reverse reaction cannot yet run and the composition is about to change.

items.q: Which statement describes what happens in the container between t<sub>2</sub> and t<sub>3</sub>?
options: XY forms and breaks apart at equal rates.
No molecules react, because the reaction is complete.
XY molecules keep forming, but XY molecules no longer break apart into X<sub>2</sub> and Y<sub>2</sub>.
X<sub>2</sub> and Y<sub>2</sub> keep reacting until one of them runs out.

why.correct: At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal and not zero. The diagrams look the same because the two reactions cancel each other's effect on the counts.
options: Right: equilibrium is dynamic. Individual XY molecules form and fall apart, but as many form as break apart in any stretch of time.
This is the static view of equilibrium. The forward and reverse reactions both continue; they just balance.
If XY only formed, its count would keep rising past 6. The count stays at 6, so XY also breaks apart.
Neither runs out: 3 of each remain at t₂ and t₃. A reversible reaction stops changing well before a reactant is used up.

items.q: Between t = 0 and t<sub>2</sub>, how many XY molecules form for each X<sub>2</sub> molecule that reacts?

why.correct: Counts change in the ratio of the coefficients: X₂ goes from 6 to 3 (−3) and XY from 0 to 6 (+6), so 2 XY per X₂.
options: Right: X₂ falls by 3 while XY rises by 6, matching the coefficients 1 and 2 in the equation.
This ignores the coefficient 2 in front of XY. Each X₂ supplies two X atoms, so it ends up in two XY molecules.
Three is how many X₂ molecules reacted, not how many XY form per X₂.
Six is the total number of XY formed. The question asks per X₂ molecule.

items.q: A student says, "At equilibrium there should be equal numbers of reactant and product molecules, so the system at t<sub>3</sub> is not at equilibrium." Which response is correct?
options: Wrong claim: equilibrium needs unchanging counts, as at t<sub>2</sub> and t<sub>3</sub>.
Right claim: there are more XY molecules than X<sub>2</sub> molecules, so the forward reaction is still ahead.
Right claim: equilibrium is reached when half of the reactant molecules have turned into product.
Wrong claim: the system is at equilibrium because the X<sub>2</sub> molecules have reacted away.

why.correct: Equilibrium means the amounts are constant over time, not that they are equal. Here the composition is the same at t₂ and t₃.
options: Right: the test for equilibrium is constant composition. The amounts can be very different from each other.
There are 3 X₂ + 3 Y₂ = 6 reactant molecules and 6 XY, but equality is not the test anyway. Constant counts are.
Nothing about equilibrium fixes it at the halfway point. Where it settles depends on the reaction and the temperature.
Three X₂ molecules remain. A system at equilibrium still holds reactants.

items.q: A sealed flask holds H<sub>2</sub>, I<sub>2</sub> and HI at equilibrium: H<sub>2</sub>(g) + I<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g). A tiny amount of I<sub>2</sub> made of a radioactive iodine isotope is swapped in for the same amount of ordinary I<sub>2</sub>, so the concentrations do not change. Later, radioactive iodine atoms are found in HI molecules. What does this show?
options: The forward reaction still runs at equilibrium.
The system was not at equilibrium before the swap.
The radioactive isotope made the forward reaction faster than the reverse reaction.
Reactions at equilibrium have stopped, and the label moved into HI molecules through mixing of the gases.

why.correct: Labeled atoms trace individual molecules. Finding the label in HI proves I₂ keeps reacting at equilibrium; HI must also keep breaking down at the same rate, since the concentrations do not change.
options: Right: the labeled I₂ could reach HI only by reacting. Constant concentrations with ongoing reaction is exactly a dynamic equilibrium.
The concentrations were constant before and after the swap. The label simply reveals reactions that were already happening.
The concentrations stay constant, so the rates stay equal. The isotope behaves chemically like ordinary iodine.
Mixing moves molecules around, but it cannot put an iodine atom inside an HI molecule. Bonds had to break and form.

items.q: Solid calcium carbonate decomposes when heated: CaCO<sub>3</sub>(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO<sub>2</sub>(g). A sample is heated in an open dish. Why does this system not reach equilibrium?
options: CO<sub>2</sub> escapes, so it rarely meets CaO to react back.
Solids are not able to take part in reversible reactions.
The forward reaction is too slow to reach equilibrium at any temperature.
Heating makes the reverse reaction faster than the forward reaction.

why.correct: A reversible reaction reaches equilibrium only in a closed system, where products stay available to react back. An open dish lets CO₂ escape.
options: Right: equilibrium needs a closed system. With the gas leaving, CO₂ can hardly ever collide with CaO to re-form CaCO₃.
Solids can react in both directions; in a sealed container this same reaction does reach equilibrium.
Speed is not the issue: the heated solid does decompose. The problem is that a product leaves the system.
If the reverse reaction were faster, CaCO₃ would form, but the open dish loses CO₂ and the solid keeps decomposing.

items.q: Pure N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> is sealed in a flask at constant temperature. Predict how each quantity changes during the first minute, before equilibrium is reached: N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NO<sub>2</sub>(g).

variables.name: Rate of the forward reaction
variables.why: The forward rate depends on [N₂O₄], which falls as N₂O₄ is used up.

variables.name: Rate of the reverse reaction
variables.why: The reverse rate depends on [NO₂], which rises from zero as NO₂ forms, so NO₂ molecules collide more often.

variables.name: [NO<sub>2</sub>]
variables.why: The forward reaction is faster than the reverse reaction, so NO₂ builds up.

variables.name: Total mass of gas in the flask
variables.why: The flask is sealed, so no atoms enter or leave; mass is conserved.

why.correct: As reactant is used up, the forward rate falls; as product builds up, the reverse rate rises. When the two meet, the concentrations stop changing.

items.q: H<sub>2</sub> and I<sub>2</sub> are sealed in a flask and react: H<sub>2</sub>(g) + I<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g). Put the events in the order they happen.
options: Only the forward reaction can occur, because no HI is present yet.
HI builds up, and HI molecules begin to react to re-form H<sub>2</sub> and I<sub>2</sub>.
The forward rate falls and the reverse rate rises as reactants are used up and HI accumulates.
The two rates become equal, and every concentration stays constant from then on.

why.correct: A reversible reaction starts with the forward rate largest and the reverse rate zero. The rates move toward each other until they are equal: that is chemical equilibrium.

items.q: A flask starts with 0.0800 M N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> and no NO<sub>2</sub>: N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NO<sub>2</sub>(g). At equilibrium, [N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>] = 0.0520 M. Calculate [NO<sub>2</sub>] at equilibrium.

mistakes.why: Value: 0.0280 M is how much N₂O₄ reacted. Each N₂O₄ gives two NO₂, so multiply by 2.
Value: you divided by 2. The coefficient 2 is on NO₂, so NO₂ rises twice as much as N₂O₄ falls.

why.correct: N₂O₄ fell by 0.0800 M − 0.0520 M = 0.0280 M. The coefficients are 1 : 2, so [NO₂] = 2 × 0.0280 M = 0.0560 M.

items.q: Which statement is true of every system at chemical equilibrium?
options: The concentrations stay constant over time.
The concentrations of reactants and products are equal.
The forward and reverse reactions have both stopped.
The reaction has gone to completion.

why.correct: At chemical equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, so the concentrations are constant. They are usually not equal.
options: Right: equal forward and reverse rates keep every amount steady.
This is the most common misconception. Equilibrium amounts can be very different; they are constant, not equal.
Both reactions continue at equal rates. That is why chemists call it dynamic.
A reaction that goes to completion uses up a reactant. At equilibrium, reactants and products are all present.

items.q: In the flask from the notes, N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NO<sub>2</sub>(g), the reverse reaction speeds up as NO<sub>2</sub> forms. Which explanation at the particle level is best?
options: More NO<sub>2</sub> per liter means more NO<sub>2</sub>-NO<sub>2</sub> collisions.
NO<sub>2</sub> molecules move faster as they form, so they collide harder.
The N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> molecules push the NO<sub>2</sub> molecules together.
The forward reaction releases energy that drives the reverse reaction.

why.correct: A reaction rate depends on how often reacting particles collide. As [NO₂] grows, NO₂-NO₂ collisions become more frequent, so the reverse rate rises.
options: Right: the reverse reaction needs two NO₂ molecules to collide. More NO₂ per liter means more such collisions each second.
Molecular speed depends on temperature, which is constant here. The change is in how many NO₂ molecules there are.
Molecules do not push others into reacting. The reverse rate depends on how often NO₂ molecules meet each other.
The reverse reaction does not need energy from the forward reaction to run; it speeds up because its reactant, NO₂, becomes more concentrated.

items.q: Which observations would tell you that a reaction in a sealed flask has reached equilibrium? Select all that apply.
options: The color of the gas mixture stops changing.
The pressure inside the flask, at constant temperature, stops changing.
The flask contains equal amounts of reactants and products.
Bubbles of gas keep forming at a steady rate in the liquid.

why.correct: Any measured property that depends on composition, such as color or (when gas moles change) pressure, becomes constant at equilibrium.
options: Right: color tracks the concentration of a colored gas, so a steady color means a steady concentration.
Right: when the number of gas molecules can change, a constant pressure means a constant composition.
Equal amounts are not the test for equilibrium. Constant amounts are.
Steady bubbling means a gas is being produced and leaving, so the composition is still changing.

items.q: What do the double half-arrows (⇌) in a chemical equation tell you?
options: The reaction can run in both directions.
The reaction is twice as fast as one written with a single arrow.
The reactants and products are present in equal amounts.
The reaction gives off heat to the surroundings.

why.correct: The ⇌ symbol shows a reversible reaction: products can react to re-form the reactants.
options: Right: the symbol marks a reversible reaction.
The symbol says nothing about speed.
The symbol says the reaction is reversible, not how much of each species is present.
Energy changes are shown with ΔH, not with the arrow.
